Course description

This course explores how to design and manage the physical, information, and financial flows that connect organizations across the supply chain. Using analytical frameworks, mathematical models, and real-world applications, you will learn to make strategic decisions related to supply chain network design, supply chain finance, supplier management and procurement, production and material requirements planning, distribution, Sales & Operations Planning (S&OP), and process and organizational design. By the end of the course you will be equipped to optimize supply chain networks, apply financial analysis to supply chain decisions, and lead cross-functional initiatives that balance operational excellence with strategic business objectives. This course is part of the MITx MicroMasters® Program in Supply Chain Management.

Practice Problem 1: MPS for Electronic Widgets
An electronic widget manufacturer is about to plan its production of a high selling widget, NOX12K678P. The demand for the widget for the next 10 weeks has been estimated as follows:
Week	Demand
1	200
2	180
3	220
4	170
5	160
6	170
7	180
8	190
9	220
10	210
TOTAL	1900
As soon as a widget is produced it is sent to the finished goods (FG) inventory. If it is shipped from the FG inventory the same week it is produced, the manufacturer assumes no inventory holding cost for the widget. However, if a widget is not shipped from the inventory the same week it is produced, a holding cost of $1 per widget is incurred for every week in inventory. As of now (end of week 0), there are 300 widgets in the FG inventory.
The setup cost to run a batch is assumed to be $1,200. The manufacturer could make all widgets in one week, so capacity is not an issue. Note that setup costs are incurred for the first batch every week independently of whether the same unit was produced in the last run of the previous week.
Part 1
0 points possible (ungraded)
What is the total cost to produce the 10 week demand for NOX12K678P if the manufacturer chooses a fixed level manufacturing strategy for the MPS? Assume that each week has one production run. Please give your answer in dollars without commas or currency symbols.

What is the total cost to produce the 10 week demand for NOX12K678P if the manufacturer chooses a Chase Demand manufacturing strategy for the MPS? The demand is considered deterministic so there is no need for a safety stock. Please give your answer in dollars without commas or currency symbols.

Sodaco runs a plant that makes and bottles private label soft drinks, sold directly to retailers. One client has recently placed an order for one of the SKUs with the following delivery schedule over the next ten weeks (one period=one week):
Period	Demand
1	3000

5	2900
6	2800
7	2800
8	2900
9	2800
10	3000
TOTAL	29600
The order is of one-time character - there are no promises for future orders from the same client.
Sodaco needs your help to create a production plan that minimizes the total costs. Costs are incurred both from holding inventory of finished goods and from changeovers in the production line. Sodaco estimates these costs according to the following:
Inventory holding costs: $0.1 per item and week
Production setup costs: $800 per production run
Any products delivered in the same week as manufactured incur no holding costs. Holding costs are then incurred for every week after the manufacturing week. Capacity is not an issue at this point.
Part 1

Part 2

Part 4
You also want to try the POQ heuristic. Assume the optimal time between runs, \(t^*\), is 4.
Using the POQ heuristic, what is the total cost for producing the ordered units? Please give your answer in dollars without commas or currency symbols.
Part 5
The Silver-Meal heuristic provides a slightly more advanced way to create a production schedule.
Using the Silver-Meal heuristic, what is the total cost for producing the ordered units? Please give your answer in dollars without commas or currency symbols.
Part 6
While the previous algorithms provide only heuristic solutions, there are several ways to find the optimal solution. For a small problem like this, the fastest way is arguably to use a spreadsheet model. Please make such a model.
According to your model, what is the minimum total cost for producing the ordered units? Please give your answer in dollars without commas or currency symbols.

Practice Problem 3: Custom Glass Inc.
Custom Glass Inc. makes custom-made windows and window frames for all types of buildings. They have just received an order from a client to make and deliver 1,340 framed windows. The windows, which are identical to one another, are to be delivered over the course of six months, according to the following schedule:
January: 300 windows
February: 280 windows
March: 200 windows
April: 190 windows
May: 160 windows
June: 210 windows
To avoid tying up too much working capital, the production manager of Custom Glass, Mr. Dumpty, is hesitant to produce all 1,340 windows at once. Not only would this tie up capital, it would also lead to a high risk obsolescence due to the rough handling in the warehouse. However, splitting up the order into several batches is also costly. For every batch they make there will be an initial setup cost due to equipment changeover and scrap from the "burn-in" period when the equipment is being fine-tuned.
Mr. Dumpty estimates the unit holding cost to be $2 per month and the setup cost to be $1,000 per batch. Week 3, Lesson 1 · Video 9: Key Take Aways OK. What are the key takeaways from this lesson? We covered a lot of ground, actually. But we kind of went really deep into one certain area. So we started off talking about master planning schedules. And we explained how that fits in with the MRP, material requirements plan, and the DRP, the distribution requirements plan. And the MPS, it's not a forecast. It's really a plan for how you're going to meet that forecast. So we'll talk later about how we get the inputs to that. But what we'll do in our next lesson is understand how the interface works between MRP systems and DRP systems. We also talked about how manufacturing strategy influences the plan. We talked about engineering to order, manufacture to order, assemble to order, and then make to stock. And so all those different plans of those different strategies dictate what it is that you're going to plan for. And we looked at different strategies, chase, level, and hybrid. Chase is where I produce exactly what I need when I need it. Level is I try to keep my production plan steady state. There's a lot of value to having stable production. But then my inventory levels will fluctuate versus a hybrid approach, which is more common where you pick and choose what makes the most sense. And we focused more on the fixed planning horizon problem. We dove pretty deep, because my real reason for diving into some of these, I wanted to expose you to two main concepts. First, the idea of heuristics in algorithms. I wanted to make you step through an algorithm, because this is what we take for granted when we throw something into a computer, because all that the computer's doing is doing a step-by-step process. And so I wanted to go through the painful details of the Silver-Meal just to make sure you understand how an algorithm works. Also, I wanted to highlight sometimes a myopic heuristic will give you a better result in practice than an optimal model. And it's mainly because optimization looks at the whole time frame and treats it all equally. And it might end up with a solution that's very brittle, that's very dependent on certain values not changing. Myopic heuristics, on the other hand, are myopic. So they only look at very close time periods. Sometimes in environments where there's a lot of change, they will give you better real world solutions.

retrieved.text: Week 3, Lesson 1 · Video 3: Fixed Planning Horizon Now let's talk about the fixed planning horizon problem. What we're trying to do is simply determine how much and when to produce or order different items. So if I look at the assumptions that I have for the inventory problem-- this is similar to other inventory models that we looked at from economic order quantity to news vendor problems-- there's certain assumptions. And what are the assumptions that are different here for the fixed planning horizon problem? Well, there are three that make it different from the traditional economic order quantity problem. The first is demand is variable. It's no longer constant. Remember in EOQ, or Economic Order Quantity, I assume that over time, if this is time, that the demand was fairly stable. Now I'm going to assume that it changes over time. So every time period, I might have a different demand. However, it's known. It's not random. So it's not like the news vendor or some of the other inventory policies we looked at. I know these and this is what I'm planning to. This is in my demand forecast. So I know for each time period how much I'm supposed to produce. Now, what else makes it different is it's a finite time period. Remember for EOQ, I'm looking for a steady state inventory policy because I assume that that condition is going to go on forever. Here, I'm planning exactly for the demand that's been forecasted for me. So at the end of this time period, I should have no inventory left, or if I have inventory left over, it's being planned for future demand. So I have a fixed or finite time period. That's why it's called the fixed planning horizon. So how are we going to talk about this? We're going to use a very simple example called the Queenstown Gyroscopes example. So your company, Queenstown Gyroscopes, just received a one-year contract with the Australian Satellite Systems Company to provide 2,000 of your special Kiwi-99 gyroscopes. And that's what this is. This is your Kiwi-99. So you have to provide 2,000 of them. And they want them at a certain time because typically, if I'm going into a system, I'm providing my product to another manufacturer, then they're not going to want them all at once. They want them spread out to match their production schedule. So in this case, month one, they want 200. And you can see this in both the chart and the table.

And for the news vendor problem, or the model, we assume a very short time period and a very high variability. But there's a lot of cases obviously in the middle, and they kind of combine both approaches. And we have two main classes where we can set up an inventory systems for each of these. And so, for the replenishment period where I'm trying to again order to determine how much to replenish and when, I've got two major classes-- continuous review and periodic review. So for the continuous review, we talked about the (s,Q) system, which is order point, order quantity-- (s,Q). And the policy is I order Q-- the amount Q-- if the inventory position is less than this trigger point, little s. OK, how much is Q? My old friend, the economic order quantity. This is Q* the EOQ that we just talked about when we assume that demand variability was relatively stable. It's a good place to start. Now, how do I set this s? What I'm saying here is my demand, or my inventory position, I track that. And if it crosses this threshold, I'm going to order Q. I'm going to order that amount up, and then inventory goes. It shows up, and the same thing happens when I cross that threshold-- I place an order. So I place an order while I'm continuously monitoring the inventory position. So how do I set s? Well, it's going to be the expected demand over lead time because if I place the order here, it's not going to show up until L time periods later. So I want to have the average, plus I want to throw in safety stock. This is Safety Stock. It's going to be some safety factor, K, that we can take off of whatever the distribution looks like, multiplied by the standard deviation of the forecast error of that lead time. So that's a continuous review policy. Pretty widely used, but even more widely used is the periodic review. This is where I will only review my inventory every R time periods. That could be once a week, every two weeks, once a month, every third day-- whatever. I have this review period every R days, and I'm going to look at that time period, look at my inventory position, and I'm going to order up to this big S. That's what's called an order up to level. Sometimes is called a par level. So I order up to, so I'd order this amount. For here, I'd order this amount, and it's whenever my review period comes up. So how much do I order? How do I set this S-- this order up to?

It's simply telling me over a period of time-- and in this example, there are six time periods. Let's call them monthly buckets. That's fairly standard-- how much my forecast is, what I'm planning to produce each period, and what I have available for my balance, what inventory I have on hand. So for this example, I've got 30 units in time zero, which is now. It's a current time. And then here in this first row, you can see what the forecasted demand is by period. And again, this is not my forecast. This is an input to the MPS. Then what I try to determine is the production plan. How much will I make in time period one, two, three, four, and so on. Now, based on that, that'll determine how much inventory I have. Because this should look familiar. It's an inventory balance equation. We've talked about this before. It's essentially a conservation of flow. So the amount of inventory I have in this time period, time period one, is going to be equal to what I had the time period before plus whatever I produce in that time period minus whatever I forecasted. Because I assume I'm taking my inventory and satisfying that demand. So all that it's telling me is that inventory has to go somewhere. It has to come from somewhere. And so it accounts for any place it can come from and go to. Now, what we want to do is come up with a production strategy to satisfy this demand. And you can see there's probably multiple ways to do this. There are two classic strategies-- level and chase. Let's talk about each of them. For level, the objective, as you would think by its name, is to keep the production level, the manufacturing, stable and level throughout the time period. How do I figure that out? Well, I look at the sum of the forecasted demand, subtract out my inventory at time zero when I start, divided by the number of periods. So in my simple example, if I look at my demand, it sums up to 90. And so I have six periods. I produced 15 each. That's shown in this chart here in this nice, stable red line. And so what does this result in? Well, if you look at time period one, I'm producing more than I need. So my inventory level is going up actually. So the inventory will not necessarily match exactly what my demand is. Because I'm producing it ahead of time in order to keep my production level. You can see the blue line here is simply the forecast.
